Value development.long:
Value development is the running record of where business is actually getting done, and how that area moves. Rather than asking where price is, it asks where price has been spending its time and volume — and whether that region is migrating up, down, or holding still.

The practical method is to look at several timeframes at once. A quarterly, monthly, weekly and daily reference each describe a different participant's idea of fair, and comparing them tells you whether the shorter-term auction agrees with the longer one. Value migrating steadily in one direction is a description of a trend that does not depend on any indicator; value flat while price swings through it describes rotation.

What makes this more useful than a trend line is that it is a statement about where volume accumulated rather than about the shape of the line, and volume is the thing that actually has to be there for a level to matter.

Where people get fooled: value development describes what has happened, not what happens next. Reading that value has migrated upward for three weeks tells you about those three weeks. Every framework built on this eventually needs a rule for when the migration stops, and the migration looks identical on the last day before it reverses as on any other day.
Value development.usage: Generally tracked across several timeframes at once to see whether the shorter-term auction agrees with the longer-term one.

VWAP standard deviation bands.long:
These plot lines a chosen number of standard deviations either side of a VWAP, giving a widening envelope that measures how far price has stretched from its volume-weighted average. Traders use them to mark where price is unusually extended and to watch what happens when it returns.

The measurement itself is real and useful. The band width is computed from the actual dispersion of trades around the average, so it adapts to conditions rather than using a fixed distance — the same virtue ATR has. A price two bands out genuinely is far from where most volume traded, and that is worth knowing.

The interpretation attached to it is where the trouble starts. The familiar figures — about 68 per cent of observations within one standard deviation, 95 within two, 99.7 within three — are properties of the normal distribution, and financial returns are not normally distributed. Benoît Mandelbrot documented this in 1963 and Eugene Fama confirmed it for equities in 1965; measured excess kurtosis for daily returns sits far above the zero a normal distribution requires, and higher still intraday.

Where people get fooled: treating a third-band touch as rare because the bell curve says it should be. Extremes arrive far more often than that arithmetic implies, which is precisely why strategies that fade the outer bands can look excellent for months and then lose more in a week than they made. The bands measure distance honestly; the probability attached to that distance is borrowed from a distribution the data does not follow.
VWAP standard deviation bands.usage: Typically used to gauge how far price has stretched from the volume-weighted average; treat the band as a distance measure, not as a probability.

Poor high / poor low.long:
A poor high is an auction extreme left flat — several periods finishing at effectively the same price, with no tapering as the market ran out of room. A poor low is the same thing underneath. The reading is that the move stopped because it ran out of time or momentum, not because it ran out of willing buyers or sellers.

The contrast is with an extreme that tapers to a point, where each successive period reached a little less far. That shape is read as the auction genuinely finishing: the last participants willing to transact up there did so, and interest thinned naturally.

Because a flat extreme suggests unfinished business, the common expectation is that price returns to it later to complete the auction. That is a description of a tendency, and it is one of the more mechanically-argued ideas in profile work, since it rests on the observable shape rather than on inferred intent.

Where people get fooled: the tendency has no timeframe attached. Price may return to a poor high in an hour, a month, or after the contract has rolled and the level no longer means anything. A prediction with no expiry cannot be wrong, which makes it comfortable to hold and useless to trade — decide in advance how long the level stays valid, or it will simply be marked correct eventually.
Poor high / poor low.usage: Generally marked as an unfinished auction extreme that price may revisit; the idea carries no timeframe unless you attach one.

Single print.long:
A single print is a price level that appears in only one time period of a profile. Everything around it traded across several periods; this level was passed through once and not revisited while the profile was building.

Mechanically it marks a stretch where price moved fast enough that two-way trade never developed — one side was aggressive enough to clear the level in a single push. That is the same market event the fair value gap describes on a candlestick chart and the imbalance describes in order-flow language: three vocabularies, one feature, drawn differently.

Because little business was done there, single prints are treated as fragile. Price returning often passes back through quickly, since there is no accumulated position at that level to defend it.

Where people get fooled: assuming the thinness predicts direction. It describes how price is likely to move through the area — quickly — not which way it will be travelling when it arrives. A thin zone accelerates a move that was already happening; it does not start one. And on a low enough timeframe almost every profile has single prints, so a rule that treats them as significant needs a size threshold stated in advance.
Single print.usage: Typically read as a thin area price may traverse quickly; the same feature a fair value gap or an imbalance describes.

TPO.long:
TPO stands for Time Price Opportunity. A TPO profile is built by dividing the session into periods and marking, for each period, every price that traded in it. Stacking those marks sideways produces a distribution whose widest part shows where price spent the most time.

The distinction from a volume profile matters and is often blurred. A TPO profile counts time — how many periods touched a price. A volume profile counts size — how much traded at a price. They usually look similar and occasionally disagree sharply, and the disagreement is the interesting part: a level with lots of time but little volume was visited repeatedly without much business being done.

The technique comes from Peter Steidlmayer's market profile work at the Chicago Board of Trade in the 1980s, developed for floor traders who could see time passing but had no live volume-at-price data. That origin explains the design: time was the available proxy.

Where people get fooled: treating the profile's shape as a forecast. It is a description of an auction that has already happened, with real explanatory value about where participants were comfortable transacting. The step from 'this is where time accumulated' to 'this is where price will return' is an inference the profile itself does not make, and profile-based rules need the same out-of-sample testing as any other.
TPO.usage: Generally used alongside a volume profile; TPO counts time at price, volume profile counts size, and their disagreements are informative.

Cumulative volume delta.long:
Delta is aggressive buying minus aggressive selling — trades that crossed the spread to hit an offer, against trades that hit a bid. Cumulative volume delta runs that total forward, producing a line showing which side has been paying up to get filled over a stretch of time.

It genuinely measures something distinct from price. Price can rise on passive buyers being filled by aggressive sellers, or on aggressive buyers lifting offers, and the delta line separates those. That distinction is not visible on a candlestick chart, which is the honest case for watching it.

The common use is disagreement: price making a new high while cumulative delta does not, taken to mean the move lacks aggressive participation. It also depends on trade classification, which is an approximation — venues report differently, and aggregating across exchanges compounds the error.

Where people get fooled: delta divergence has exactly the freedom that indicator divergence has. It appears constantly inside healthy trends, it can persist for a long time before anything happens, and which swing you compare against is chosen after the fact. Someone reviewing a chart will find the divergence that preceded the reversal and not the eight that preceded nothing. Fix the comparison rule before judging it, and count every occurrence.
Cumulative volume delta.usage: Typically read for disagreement between price and aggressive participation; classification is approximate and divergences are common inside trends.

Normal distribution.long:
The normal distribution — the bell curve, also called the Gaussian — describes data clustering symmetrically around an average, with roughly 68 per cent of observations inside one standard deviation, 95 inside two and 99.7 inside three. Human height is the textbook example: most adults near the average, progressively fewer toward the extremes.

It is the assumption underneath most statistical tools drawn on a chart. Standard deviation bands, confidence intervals, Sharpe ratios and value-at-risk calculations all inherit it, usually without saying so.

Financial returns do not follow it. Benoît Mandelbrot showed this in 1963 in The Variation of Certain Speculative Prices, and Eugene Fama confirmed it for equities in 1965. Measured excess kurtosis — which is zero for a normal distribution — runs far above zero for daily returns and higher again intraday, meaning the tails are much fatter than the curve allows. Days that the bell curve calls once-in-a-lifetime turn up every few years.

Where people get fooled: the percentages get quoted about price as though they were measured rather than assumed. A three-standard-deviation move is not a one-in-several-hundred event in markets, and any tool that implies it is understating exactly the risk that ends accounts. The distribution is a useful approximation in the middle and dangerously wrong in the tails, which is the only region where it really matters.
Normal distribution.usage: Generally the unstated assumption behind standard-deviation bands and risk measures; the middle is a fair approximation, the tails are not.
